title: Draupadi's sari
hookLine: Draupadi's question, and the cloth that wouldn't end
carry: krishna answers the one who calls

lines: LOST IN A GAME SHE WASN'T PLAYING.
cards: Draupadi isn't even in the hall. She's in the women's rooms when a servant comes to tell her she's been lost in a game she wasn't playing: she now belongs to the Kauravas, and must come.
Instead of coming, she sends back a question. It's a sharp question, and nobody in that hall, not the kings, not the elders, can answer it.
This is a hard scene, about a woman humiliated in public, so i'll tell it carefully.

teach.b: Her question: when Yudhishthira staked me, had he already lost himself? If he had, he was a slave, and what right does a slave have to stake anyone?
Duryodhana doesn't answer. He sends his brother Dushasana, who drags her into the hall by her hair. Before the whole court, Draupadi asks again.
The grandfather Bhishma, the elder everyone looks to, says the ways of dharma are subtle, and he can't say.

Only one of the hundred Kaurava brothers, the young Vikarna, stands up and says she's right, and he's shouted down. Dushasana is ordered to strip her, in front of everyone. He grabs the end of her garment and pulls.
And pulls. The cloth keeps coming, yard after yard, until Dushasana collapses, exhausted, and Draupadi is still standing, still covered.
In the popular telling, she has called on Krishna, and he answers her with cloth that never ends.
In a version many devotees love, she holds her sari tight at first, and only when she lets go and raises both hands to call him does the cloth start to flow.
That's why this scene sits at the heart of bhakti, loving devotion: when the elders fail and no hand in the hall will help, the one who calls on God isn't left alone.
The one who was supposed to be shamed is the one left standing. Bhima swears a terrible vow of revenge. Jackals howl, a bad omen.
The blind king, frightened, finally offers Draupadi wishes, and she uses them to free her husbands. Her question was never answered. Her dignity was never removed.

how: Draupadi's disrobing and the unending cloth are retold again and again in dance, theater and devotional song; devotees see in it Krishna's protection of those who call on him, and in parts of south India Draupadi herself is worshiped as a goddess.

o: the cloth that kept coming, so she stayed covered
a wedding gift that won the Pandavas a kingdom
a silk banner the Pandavas carried into battle

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: asked if he'd already lost himself
said the ways of dharma are subtle
the one Kaurava who spoke for her

s: someone in the hall answered Draupadi's question
nobody did. even Bhishma said the ways of dharma were too subtle to say.
one of the hundred Kaurava brothers spoke up for her
the young Vikarna said she was right, and was shouted down.
every version tells the miracle exactly the same way
the popular telling has her call on Krishna; other tellings say it more briefly.

games.q: you're Draupadi, dragged into the hall. the elders are silent, and Dushasana grabs your sari. in the popular telling, what do you do?
games.why: she calls on Krishna, and the cloth keeps coming until Dushasana collapses. devotees still tell it to show that God answers the one who calls.

practice: Sit with your spine straight, the way Draupadi stood. Remember a time no one in the room would speak up for you. Draupadi's answer, in the telling devotees love, was to call a name.
Many Hindus still do: Krishna, Govinda, Ram, whispered in a waiting room or before a hard phone call. If you pray, say the name you pray to, slowly, three times, and hand over what you can't hold.
If you don't, name one person who'd stand with you.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi's sari. The cloth that wouldn't end, and a question the whole court couldn't answer.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Draupadi, 'daughter of Drupada', the king of Panchala.

carryVoice: Your line: Krishna answers the one who calls. Draupadi called, and the cloth kept coming. That's day seventy-three.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (Draupadi's question; Vikarna; the disrobing; Bhima's vow; Dhritarashtra's boons)
